content: Evidence synthesis is necessary, and the topic along with the newly synthesized evidence must be reviewed by the Guideline Development Group (GDG). This review process includes a comprehensive application of the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework. This framework allows for modifications to the strength of existing recommendations based on new evidence. The Mental Health Gap Action Programme (mhGAP) guidelines for mental, neurological, and substance use disorders were updated, and the Technical Expert Group (TEG) was tasked with identifying new questions that should be considered. Module focal points and the Secretariat prepared a summary report, which included suggested actions for each recommendation and proposed new questions informed by TEG discussions. The 2015 mhGAP guideline contained 120 recommendations across 10 modules. Based on field requests and the increasing burden of anxiety disorders, the Secretariat identified the need for a new module on anxiety (ANX). A focal point was assigned to this module, and a TEG was convened to propose and discuss new questions. Eleven summary documents, based on TEG suggestions for each module, were shared with the WHO Steering Group and the GDG for review. The Steering Group also evaluated whether the new questions were already addressed in other WHO guidelines. Evidence retrieval and synthesis followed the methods outlined in the WHO handbook for guideline development. Key questions and recommendations were identified using the PICO framework (Population, Intervention, Comparator, Outcome), and systematic reviews were conducted to provide evidence for each outcome. GRADE profiles were prepared for each question, and the quality of both quantitative and qualitative evidence was appraised. Two online scoping meetings with GDG members in September 2021 led to the identification of 50 research questions for the update, including 31 updated questions from the 2015 mhGAP guideline and 19 new questions (seven of which focused on anxiety). The PICO framework was used to define these questions, specifying critical and important outcomes. For updated questions, the outcomes specified in the 2015 guideline were used as the basis for the updated and new questions. Evidence to support the guideline was extracted from various sources by evidence review and synthesis teams in collaboration with the Steering Group. Standard protocols were developed, including clear review questions, criteria for study identification, search strategies for bibliographic databases, methods for assessing risk of bias, and a data analysis plan. These protocols were reviewed and endorsed by the guideline methodologist, coordinating team, and Steering Group members. Evidence was retrieved according to standard operating procedures, formats, and timelines provided by the Steering Group. Both quantitative and qualitative evidence were considered. Quantitative evidence on the effectiveness of interventions was primarily extracted from Cochrane Reviews and other systematic reviews. If reviews were outdated (more than two years old), they were updated. The COVID-19 pandemic caused delays in mental, neurological, and substance use disorder research, potentially affecting the availability of systematic reviews within the preferred two-year period. New systematic reviews were conducted when none were available. Resource and cost considerations were included in the implementation details of each recommendation. Qualitative reviews focused on the experiences of end users and health workers, including barriers and facilitators to intervention uptake, acceptability, feasibility, and perceptions of equity. Evidence on these issues was synthesized through qualitative reviews addressing questions such as: What are end users’ experiences of receiving care for mental, neurological, and substance use disorders in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs)? What are health workers’ views and experiences of providing care for these disorders in LMICs? These reviews were informed by two systematic reviews on the use of mhGAP and country case studies on mhGAP implementation. The findings from qualitative and quantitative reviews, along with systematic reviews on mhGAP use and case studies, informed GDG discussions on the mhGAP guideline. These discussions considered domains of the GRADE EtD framework, including values, health equity, equality, non-discrimination, human rights, sociocultural acceptability, and feasibility. The GRADE approach was used to appraise the quality of quantitative evidence for all critical outcomes identified in the PICO questions. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were considered high-quality evidence, while non-randomized trials and observational studies were considered low-quality evidence. Quality ratings could be downgraded based on study design limitations, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. Conversely, observational studies could be upgraded based on factors such as the magnitude of effect if no limitations warranted downgrading. Systematic review teams and the guideline methodologist synthesized evidence according to the WHO handbook for guideline development. Outcomes were presented as meta-analyses when possible; otherwise, narrative syntheses were conducted. Qualitative evidence was appraised using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Checklist for Systematic Reviews. Evidence summaries for each priority question were drafted by evidence review and synthesis teams, populating relevant sections of the GRADE EtD frameworks. The Steering Group reviewed these summaries and profiles in collaboration with the evidence review teams and guideline methodologist, presenting them to the GDG during a series of meetings. GDG meetings occurred between June and November 2022, including virtual and hybrid formats. Evidence summaries and pre-recorded presentations were provided to GDG members in advance. During the meetings, evidence was presented, and GDG members reached consensus on the rating for each EtD element. Draft recommendations were formulated by consensus, defined as full agreement among all GDG participants when possible. If consensus could not be reached, decisions were put to a vote, requiring a large majority (more than two-thirds) for approval. Following these processes, the Steering Group circulated draft recommendations to GDG members for further comment. A full draft of the guideline document, including recommendations and supporting evidence, was sent to the External Review Group (ERG) for review. Comments from the Steering Group, GDG, and ERG were collated to revise the draft. This guideline includes 48 updated and new evidence-based recommendations related to mental, neurological, and substance use conditions. These are based on 30 updated PICO questions from the 2015 mhGAP guideline and 18 new PICO questions developed for this edition. For some questions, insufficient evidence was available to support new or updated recommendations, so pre-existing recommendations were endorsed. Each recommendation includes justification, remarks, research gaps, and implementation considerations. The evidence profiles are available online. The updated and new recommendations complement 90 pre-existing guideline recommendations, which remain validated and endorsed in their current format.
